content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.7, using 46 of the 60 budget. The test results were very noisy (the same task ranged from 1 to 50 examples), so the evidence points one way but isn't decisive.

**Phase 1.** I trained L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3, so each of those nine rules had been seen once. Then I tested three new tasks, each 8–10 times:

| Probe | Rules not yet trained | Highest overlap with a trained task | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S2-M3 | 0 | 0.375 | ≈22 |
| L1-S1-M4 | 1 | 0.75 | ≈19 |
| L4-S4-M4 | 3 | 0.56 | ≈25 |

For reference, an already-trained task averaged about 8 and an untrained task about 60 (from only two samples). A part-based learner should have found L1-S2-M3 nearly as easy as a trained task and L4-S4-M4 nearly as hard as an untrained one. Instead the two were about equal. That makes part-based unlikely.

**Phase 2.** I trained four more tasks (L2-S2-M3, L1-S2-M1, L1-S3-M1, L2-S1-M3). This brought L1, S2 and M3 to three appearances each, while keeping L1-S2-M3's closest overlap at 0.375. A factor-when-justified learner (k = 2 or 3) would have turned those rules into parts, so L1-S2-M3 should then have become cheap. It stayed at about 26 over 6 tests, which argues against factor-when-justified.

What remains fits holistic: every probe was well below the untrained cost, and the task with the highest overlap (L1-S1-M4) was the cheapest. That ordering is only slightly better than chance given the noise, so the case against the other two is stronger than the direct support for holistic.
